desc:
The height of a node is the number of edges on the longest downward path from that node to a leaf in its own subtree. A leaf has height 0.

Return the sum of the heights of all nodes of the tree. The empty tree gives 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 9, 20, -1, -1, 15, 7] the heights are 2 (root), 0, 1, 0, 0, so the answer is 3. For the chain [1, 2, -1, 3] the heights are 2, 1, 0 and the answer is 3.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Computing the height of each node separately from scratch would be O(n<sup>2</sup>) on a long chain. Look for a way to reuse results.
The height of a node depends only on the heights of its two children.
Process nodes from the last one back to the first (children come after their parent in level order): h[k] = 1 + max(h[left], h[right]) with a missing child counting as -1, then sum all h.
editorial: The height of a node is 0 for a leaf and 1 + max(height(left), height(right)) otherwise. If you treat a missing child as height -1 the two cases merge into one formula.

Heights must be computed bottom-up so each node's value is known when its parent needs it. In the level-order array all children come after their parent, so a single backward pass over the real nodes does it. Adding every height as you go gives the answer in O(n) total, instead of O(n<sup>2</sup>) for the approach that recomputes a height for every node.
The largest possible answer (a path of 1,500 nodes) is about 1.1 million, which fits easily.
